title: How to stay afloat this tire season
summary: Prepare for dealership tire season by contacting stored-tire customers early, pacing appointments to shop capacity, and keeping peak service calls moving.
body_markdown:
Tire season can overwhelm a dealership before the first fully booked day. Customers with stored tires want appointments. New callers need answers. Advisors are checking in vehicles while the phone queue grows. If the store waits for that rush to begin, the schedule and the service team both become harder to manage.


The practical answer is to work backward from capacity. Confirm how many tire visits the shop can fulfill, contact stored-tire customers before the rush in batches that fit those openings, and give incoming calls a clear path to a booking or an owned next step. This plan works for spring and fall changeovers.


It is one part of a broader[fixed operations service workflow](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/pillars/ai-service-advisor) : answer demand, book within real capacity, and keep exceptions with the right employee.


## Set tire season capacity before you contact anyone


Start with the service schedule, not the customer list. Decide how many tire appointments each day can realistically support after accounting for technicians, bays, equipment, storage retrieval, and the other work your shop must still complete.


A simple worksheet is enough:


Capacity question Store answer


How many tire appointment slots are approved each day? Use the service scheduler's real appointment types and staffing plan.


How many are already booked? Include phone, online, and advisor-created appointments.


What capacity must stay available for other service work or disruptions? Set the buffer using your own operating plan.


How many slots can outbound outreach offer? Approved tire slots minus existing bookings and the buffer.


Then reconcile the stored-tire records. Check which sets are at the dealership or storage provider, which vehicle each set belongs to, how long retrieval takes, and whether a condition or fitment question needs staff review. A stored set with an uncertain location should not be treated as ready for tomorrow's appointment.


This connection between storage and service capacity matters.[Canadian Auto Dealer's discussion of the tire storage business](https://canadianautodealer.ca/2021/04/maximize-your-tire-season-revenue/) describes how changeovers bring customers back to the dealership. Operationally, each return visit also needs a real slot and a ready tire set.


## Call stored-tire customers before the rush


Stored-tire customers are a known audience for seasonal outreach, but calling or messaging the entire list at once can create the very bottleneck you are trying to avoid. Build an eligible list from verified storage records. Remove customers who already booked, duplicate vehicle records, and anyone who should not receive the chosen channel. Put unresolved storage or vehicle matches on a staff review list.


Release outreach in batches against available appointment capacity. If one week has openings and the next is full, direct the first batch to the open week. Pause or shrink the next batch when replies, bookings, or staff callbacks begin to outpace what the store can handle. The aim is to fill the schedule intentionally, not create a burst of calls for dates you cannot offer.


For customers who prefer the phone, make outbound calls while good appointment choices remain. Use approved texts or emails for customers eligible for those channels, and give every reply a booking path. A call that reaches voicemail should not trigger an endless series of duplicate touches; define the next attempt and stop conditions before launch.


[Clearline Campaigns](https://www.useclearline.com/product/campaigns) can contact an approved list of stored-tire customers by phone, text, or email before the rush and move interested customers toward a booking. Tie each outreach batch to the store's open tire appointments so the campaign fills days the shop can actually serve, without asking advisors to make every reminder call.


Keep the message specific and easy to act on:


> Hi \[first name\], it's \[dealership\]. We're scheduling seasonal tire changes for customers with stored tires. Would you like us to find a time for your \[vehicle\]? Reply here or call \[service number\].


Use the correct vehicle and storage record before personalizing. If the set is not ready, do not imply it is. Stop the sequence once the customer books, declines, or opts out. For Canadian commercial email and text campaigns, the[CRTC's CASL guidance](https://crtc.gc.ca/eng/com500/faq500.htm) explains consent, sender identification, and unsubscribe requirements; have the dealership's legal owner approve the audience and channel rules.


## Protect the service line when tire appointment calls rise


Early outreach smooths the schedule, but inbound demand will still rise when customers decide it is time to swap tires. Decide before the peak when additional coverage answers: after hours, after an unanswered ring period, or when the live queue reaches a threshold. Test the exact behavior with your phone provider and actual staffing plan. A transfer that loops a caller back into the same full queue does not help.


[Clearline Inbound](https://www.useclearline.com/product/inbound) can answer when the service team is tied up or the store is closed, identify a tire appointment request, and book an eligible time when the calendar connection and store rules allow it. Calls about storage problems, fitment, pricing, or safety still reach a person with the conversation context. That gives routine callers a next step without adding another call to an advisor's queue.


Give every tire call a defined outcome:


Caller needs First action When a person takes over


A routine tire change Check the approved appointment type and live availability; book only after the system confirms it. The customer or vehicle cannot be matched, or the required slot is unavailable.


A change to an existing booking Verify the appointment and apply the store's rescheduling rules. The change conflicts with retrieval timing or shop capacity.


A question about stored tires Answer only from an approved storage status and preparation instructions. The set is missing, not ready, or its condition is uncertain.


Tire condition, fitment, price, or a safety concern Capture the details and route to the right employee. Immediately, under the dealership's escalation rules.


A request for an advisor Transfer with the conversation context. Whenever the customer asks.


An answered call is not necessarily a booked appointment. If the scheduler cannot confirm a slot, call it a request and tell the customer who will follow up. The[service call overflow guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/dealership-service-call-overflow) has a fuller routing and fallback model.


## Keep exceptions out of the advisor's phone queue


The point of call coverage is to let advisors focus on vehicles in the drive and the questions that need judgment. Give each exception a primary owner, a backup, and a due time. Common tire season exceptions include an unmatched stored set, a worn or damaged tire, a fitment concern, variable pricing, an unavailable appointment, a failed transfer, or an upset customer.


The handoff should carry the customer's name, vehicle, requested work, preferred time, stored-set reference if available, and what has already been attempted. The customer should hear a concrete next step. “The tire coordinator will call you back after checking the storage record” is useful; “someone will get back to you” is not.


Before the next day's arrivals, compare confirmed appointments with retrieval status and outstanding exceptions. A booking with no ready set needs action while there is still time to contact the customer. For more detail on what counts as a confirmed booking, use the[service appointment scheduling guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/automate-service-appointment-scheduling-dealerships) .


## Use a short daily tire season control check


Seasonal plans need daily adjustment. A brief morning check should cover expected arrivals, tire sets ready for retrieval, open slots, staff coverage, and callbacks due. At midday, look at the call queue and whether outreach should continue. At close, reconcile what was booked, what is still a request, and what needs an owner tomorrow.


Track a small set of measures by day and hour:


Measure What to count


Call answer rate Tire-related calls answered divided by tire-related calls offered.


Wait and hold time The median and 90th percentile waits during peak hours, using your phone system's reporting.


Confirmed tire bookings Appointments that exist in the approved scheduler, separate from callback requests.


Outreach-to-booking rate Confirmed bookings from eligible stored-tire customers divided by customers reached.


Unowned exceptions Requests that still lack a named employee or completed next step.


Arrival rate Customers who arrive divided by confirmed tire appointments.


Use your own baseline to set targets. If hold times climb while the calendar is full, more outreach will add pressure. If open slots remain and calls are under control, another small batch may help. The manager's decision should follow both shop capacity and the customer queue.

## Frequently asked questions


### When should a dealership contact customers with stored tires?


Contact them before the expected appointment rush, once you know which sets are ready and which dates the shop can serve. The right lead time depends on your storage retrieval process and local demand. Send outreach in batches tied to open slots.


### What if every tire appointment is full?


Offer the next approved opening or create an owned request for staff review. Do not promise an exception slot or call a request a confirmed appointment.


### Which tire season calls need an advisor?


Send condition, fitment, safety, variable pricing, complaints, and explicit requests for a person to the appropriate employee. Routine booking and status questions can follow approved rules when the data is available.
